builder_plan.scenario: Tool errors or unavailable services cause your agent to abandon recoverable tasks.
builder_plan.change: Inject repeatable tool failures and change only the recovery policy.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current retry and fallback behavior under the same injected failures.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Recovered tasks, duplicate side effects, retries, time to recovery, and total cost.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Which Hand Was Late? Diagnosis for Robot Failure Recovery in Bimanual Tool Use
summary: The technique replaces failure diagnosers trained on single-arm perturbations with a VLM-based diagnoser that analyzes bimanual tool-use failures, paired with an escalation-based repair policy. It costs the engineering effort of instrumenting robot sensing channels and querying a VLM, plus latency for diagnosis, and requires access to robot execution traces that the reader's general AI/ML practice likely lacks. It can fail because identifiability limits are fundamental: whether a late attempt was also pushed too weakly is not identifiable from passive sensing when the tool hand is late, and the VLM's verbal answer depends on question wording despite its internal state encoding the late hand.
rationale: This is a robotics-specific failure diagnosis study in simulation with no direct applicability or quantified efficiency gain for an AI/ML engineer working under standard LLM infrastructure constraints.
technique: VLM-Based Diagnosis for Bimanual Failure Recovery

claims.statement: The technique replaces failure diagnosers trained on single-arm perturbations with a VLM-based diagnoser that analyzes bimanual tool-use failures, paired with an escalation-based repair policy. It costs the engineering effort of instrumenting robot sensing channels and querying a VLM, plus latency for diagnosis, and requires access to robot execution traces that the reader's general AI/ML practice likely lacks. It can fail because identifiability limits are fundamental: whether a late attempt was also pushed too weakly is not identifiable from passive sensing when the tool hand is late, and the VLM's verbal answer depends on question wording despite its internal state encoding the late hand.
A repair policy that escalates when the cause is not identifiable repairs as many failures as one given the true cause, within two attempts.
